title: You’ve Been Thinking About This Verse Wrong: What “Set Your Mind on Things Above” Really Means
paragraphs: You’ve Been Thinking About This Verse Wrong: What “Set Your Mind on Things Above” Really Means

Paul was not telling you to escape your problems, suppress your pain, or spend every waking moment thinking about heaven. He was telling people who had been raised with Christ to learn how to see everything—including suffering, temptation, money, relationships, failure, success, and tomorrow—from where Christ now reigns.
There is a strange kind of exhaustion that comes from living with your body in one place and your mind in ten others.
You are sitting at dinner, but your mind is replaying what somebody said.
You are lying in bed, but your mind is already fighting tomorrow.
You are worshiping, but part of you is calculating bills.
You are praying, but underneath the prayer is fear.
You open Scripture, but your thoughts keep wandering toward the person who hurt you.
And nobody realizes there is an entire war happening behind your eyes.
Maybe that is why these words of Paul have been repeated so often:

But that interpretation becomes dangerous when it turns Christianity into spiritual escapism—as though following Jesus means becoming less concerned about the brokenness around us, less emotionally honest about suffering, or somehow detached from ordinary responsibilities.
That is not what Paul wrote.
And when you see what he actually said, this familiar verse becomes far more demanding—and far more beautiful.
The New Testament was written here in Greek, not Hebrew or Aramaic, so the Greek wording matters. Colossians 3:1–2 reads:
Εἰ οὖν συνηγέρθητε τῷ Χριστῷ, τὰ ἄνω ζητεῖτε... τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε, μὴ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.
“If, then, you were raised together with Christ, keep seeking the things above... Set your minds on the things above, not on the things upon the earth.”
The phrase sitting at the heart of the passage is:
τὰ ἄνω φρονεῖτε — ta anō phroneite.
But phroneite, from the Greek verb phroneō, reaches beyond the modern idea of having an occasional thought.
It carries the sense of setting one’s mind or orientation upon something—directing the inner outlook that shapes how a person understands and lives.
Paul is talking about the governing orientation of your life.
And notice something even more important.
Paul does not merely say, “Think about heaven.”
“…where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.”
Paul's command is anchored in the enthroned Jesus.
The One who was rejected is reigning.
The One who was crucified is alive.
The One who carried our sins has conquered death.
So setting your mind above means learning to interpret the world below in light of the Christ who reigns above.
That means your circumstances do not get the final word.
Your feelings do not get the final word.
Your temptation does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Your bank account does not get the final word.
Your reputation does not get the final word.
Your worst failure does not get the final word.
Death itself does not get the final word.
And perhaps this is where the verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us have not merely been thinking about earthly things.
We have been allowing earthly things to tell us who we are.
One person succeeds while we struggle:
One terrible chapter from our past resurfaces:
That is who I really am.
We may believe in Jesus intellectually while allowing circumstances to disciple our imagination.
Not because the pain is imaginary.
Not because the bills are imaginary.
Not because betrayal does not hurt.
Look again because there is a greater reality than what your frightened eyes can presently see.
And then Paul says something astonishing:
“For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” (Colossians 3:3)
Your life is hidden with Christ in God.
Not hidden in your relationship status.
Not hidden in how attractive you feel today.
Not hidden in how many people applaud you.
Not hidden in your ministry statistics.
Not hidden in whether the person who abandoned you ever realizes what they lost.
Paul is describing an identity so securely joined to Jesus that the world cannot accurately measure its worth.
Maybe you desperately need that truth because you have spent years trying to prove yourself.
Proving that the divorce did not destroy you.
Proving that the rejection did not hurt.
Proving that you are spiritually strong.
Please tell me I am enough.
Then the Gospel walks into the room and does something completely different.
You are a sinner who cannot rescue yourself.

Sin is not merely an unfortunate habit. It is rebellion against the holy God who made us. Scripture does not diagnose humanity as basically good people needing better motivation. We need reconciliation. We need forgiveness. We need resurrection.
The righteous One stood where the guilty belonged.
Jesus bore sin upon the cross.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives something achievement could never purchase:
That is why Paul's command begins with something God has already done.
“If then you have been raised with Christ…”
Set your mind correctly so that perhaps Christ will accept you.
Because you belong to the risen Christ, begin thinking like someone whose entire existence has been changed by Him.
The Gospel does not say, “Climb high enough and maybe Jesus will receive you.”
Jesus comes down into our scandal, bears our guilt at Calvary, rises victorious, and brings repentant sinners into His life.
And this is where “set your mind on things above” stops being a decorative Christian quotation and starts interfering with your life.
Because Paul does not allow heavenly-mindedness to remain theoretical.
After telling believers to set their minds above, Paul immediately begins talking about what must die below.
In other words, thinking about “things above” does not make you useless on earth.
It changes the way you live on earth.
The person whose mind is fixed upon Christ should become more honest, not less.
More capable of loving difficult people.
Heavenly-mindedness is not staring at the clouds while your family suffers beside you.
It is bringing the character of the reigning Christ into your kitchen.
That is where this verse becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the earthly thing consuming our minds is not money.
And you keep returning to the courtroom inside your imagination.
And slowly, without realizing it, the person who wounded you begins occupying mental territory that belongs to Christ.
Setting your mind above does not mean pretending the injustice never happened.
Jesus never teaches us to call evil good.
It means remembering that Christ is Judge, Christ is Lord, Christ knows the truth, and your wounded heart does not have to become a prison where the offender lives rent-free forever.
Sometimes the earthly thing is lust.
You tell yourself it is private.
But your mind is learning to desire what Christ died to free you from.
Setting your mind above means bringing even your sexuality under the lordship of Jesus.
Not merely asking, “Can I get away with this?”
“Does this belong to the life of the risen Christ?”
Sometimes the earthly thing is success.
This one hides well in churches.
But underneath the spiritual vocabulary can live the same ancient hunger:
And you can spend your life building something “for God” while secretly needing people to worship the builder.
Would you still obey Me if nobody applauded?
Would you still serve if somebody else received the credit?
Would you still preach if there were twenty people instead of twenty thousand?
Would you still give if your name never appeared?
Because “things above” are not merely Christian activities.
Things above are realities governed by Christ.
This is also why setting your mind above cannot mean ignoring suffering.
Scripture never commands believers to become emotionally numb.
There are days when setting your mind on Christ may happen while tears are falling.
Still wake at 3:00 a.m. wondering what God is doing.
Faith does not always sound like shouting.
Jesus, I don't understand this, but I still belong to You.
Sometimes setting your mind above means refusing to interpret God's character through one terrible Tuesday.
It means interpreting Tuesday through the cross and resurrection.
The cross tells you God has entered human suffering.
The empty tomb tells you suffering will not reign forever.
And Christ's promised appearing tells you history is going somewhere.
That is exactly where Paul takes the passage:
“When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” (Colossians 3:4)
Not Christ who helps your life.
Not Christ who improves your life.
Not Christ who occupies the religious section of your life.
That may be the most confronting sentence in this entire article.
Because many of us want Jesus to bless our life.
Paul describes Jesus as our life.
One keeps Christ as an accessory.
The other places Him at the center.
And maybe that is the question waiting underneath everything:
If Jesus were removed from your Christianity, how much of your life would actually change?
Would you still have your ambitions?
Or would everything collapse because Christ Himself was the center holding it together?
“Set your mind on things above” means Jesus is becoming the reference point from which everything else receives its proper value.
But Jesus is Lord over relationships.
But work is not your identity.
But appearance is not your god.
But pain is not your prophet.
But fear does not own it.
But resurrection has changed what death means for those in Christ.
This is why Paul can speak with such confidence.
The Christian's deepest life is hidden somewhere suffering cannot ultimately reach.
Maybe tonight your life does not look impressive.
Maybe nobody knows how difficult this season has been.
Maybe you have disappointed yourself again.
Maybe you are fighting a temptation you thought you would have defeated years ago.
Maybe your faith feels smaller than it used to.
Then hear the Gospel before you hear another motivational speech.
Jesus is not asking you to save yourself.
Stop negotiating with the sin He is exposing.
Stop decorating what needs to die.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop allowing shame to convince you that hiding from Christ is safer than running toward Him.
Bring the scandal into His light.
The cross already proves that Jesus knows exactly how ugly sin is.
And the cross also proves how far He went to redeem sinners.
There is grace for the repentant.
You do not have to manufacture a cleaner past before approaching Jesus.
Bring Him the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
He is still the Savior who turns graves into testimonies.
From scandal to grace, Jesus is still rewriting people.
And tomorrow morning, your mind will probably wander again.
That is why Paul's words are not a one-time emotional experience.
The Christ who is your life.
And if something in these words exposed what has been occupying your mind lately, do not rush away from that conviction.
And be honest with other believers.
Sometimes two words are enough to stop hiding.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if the truth of Christ has helped you, sharing it can be one simple way of putting encouragement in front of somebody who may desperately need it.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too—not merely to grow a page, but because people need Scripture, conviction, encouragement, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and above all, Jesus Christ.

Supporting Gospel ministry is not a way to purchase God's blessing, prove that you glorify Him, or earn spiritual merit. Scripture does, however, teach believers to use their resources generously for God's purposes.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So tonight, when the world tries once more to tell you who you are, remember Paul's words.
Not because earth does not matter.
But because you will never understand life below correctly until you see it beneath the throne of the One above.
Your scandal may explain where you have been.
Your wounds may explain why you hurt.
Your failures may explain some of your consequences.
But none of them has the authority to write the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.

The loudest thing in your mind does not have to become the lord of your life—because above every fear, every failure, every grave, and every unfinished chapter, Jesus Christ is still seated on the throne.
